items.title: Carol Bash interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 2, 2012
items.q: I was like I’d never heard of her. And I knew jazz, I mean the names. But I had never heard of her.

ctx.x: It’s nice that you’re focusing on Mary Lou Williams, a person who doesn’t show up in the history books as often as she should. Is that something that drove you to do this.

Yeah, absolutely. When I first came to Mary Lou, basically it was through her music. And I was at my in-laws’ house. My husband is also a Hamilton alum. But anyway, I was in their house and my father-in-law was playing Mary Lou Williams on the stereo, and I just was bowled over by her music. And I asked him who is this playing, and he said Mary Lou Williams, she’s one of the greats. And I was like I’d never heard of her. And I knew jazz, I mean the names. But I had never heard of her. And when a book came out…

Yeah. It’s serendipitous that that book came out, sort of like the planets aligned a little bit for you. I found it interesting, I have to admit too that I didn’t know enough about her when your film came up and then I took out some music to listen to. And her solo piano playing had a touch of really raw basic blues, almost like to the point of, I almost felt like she was even an older soul playing stuff from the turn of the century almost. It’s very interesting.

items.q: I’m trying to do with the film is to tell her story through her words... creating a script based on that.

ctx.x: Yeah. It’s serendipitous that that book came out, sort of like the planets aligned a little bit for you. I found it interesting, I have to admit too that I didn’t know enough about her when your film came up and then I took out some music to listen to. And her solo piano playing had a touch of really raw basic blues, almost like to the point of, I almost felt like she was even an older soul playing stuff from the turn of the century almost. It’s very interesting.

Um hum. Well you know that’s her philosophy. Her philosophy about jazz is that it came from the blues, it came from the suffering of black people. And she said without the blues there is no jazz. So it’s all about the blues for Mary Lou, and yeah, it just resonates throughout no matter what style she’s playing, because you know she plays so many © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-
styles. But whatever it is, you know, she still has that blues kind of heavy duty rhythm and beat to her music, that makes it swing.
